claim: Zebrafish have made significant contributions to our understanding of the vertebrate brain and the neural basis of behavior.
source: Zebrafish have made significant contributions to our understanding of the vertebrate brain and the neural basis of behavior, earning a place as one of the most widely used model organisms in neuroscience.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field's consensus on zebrafish contributions, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Zebrafish are one of the most widely used model organisms in neuroscience.
source: Zebrafish have made significant contributions to our understanding of the vertebrate brain and the neural basis of behavior, earning a place as one of the most widely used model organisms in neuroscience.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the prevalence of zebrafish in neuroscience research.

claim: The appeal of zebrafish arises from the marriage of low cost, early life transparency, and ease of genetic manipulation with a behavioral repertoire that becomes more sophisticated as animals transition from larvae to adults.
source: Their appeal arises from the marriage of low cost, early life transparency, and ease of genetic manipulation with a behavioral repertoire that becomes more sophisticated as animals transition from larvae to adults.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about the advantages of zebrafish as a model organism.

claim: AZBA is the first fully segmented three-dimensional digital adult zebrafish brain atlas.
source: To further enhance the use of adult zebrafish, we created the first fully segmented three-dimensional digital adult zebrafish brain atlas (AZBA).
evidence: This is a direct claim about the novelty of the work presented in the manuscript.

claim: AZBA was built by combining tissue clearing, light-sheet fluorescence microscopy, and three-dimensional image registration of nuclear and antibody stains.
source: AZBA was built by combining tissue clearing, light-sheet fluorescence microscopy, and three-dimensional image registration of nuclear and antibody stains.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, which is documented in the manuscript.

claim: AZBA images were used to guide segmentation of the atlas into over 200 neuroanatomical regions comprising the entirety of the adult zebrafish brain.
source: These images were used to guide segmentation of the atlas into over 200 neuroanatomical regions comprising the entirety of the adult zebrafish brain.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data and results of the segmentation process.

claim: AZBA is an open source, online, updatable digital resource.
source: As an open source, online (azba.wayne.edu), updatable digital resource, AZBA will significantly enhance the use of adult zebrafish in furthering our understanding of vertebrate brain function in both health and disease.
evidence: This describes the accessibility and nature of the resource created.

claim: AZBA will significantly enhance the use of adult zebrafish in furthering our understanding of vertebrate brain function in both health and disease.

claim: Zebrafish were originally established as a model organism for developmental biology due to ease of domestication, high fecundity, and early life transparency.
source: Originally established as a model organism for developmental biology due to ease of domestication, high fecundity, and early life transparency (Parichy, 2015), the increased popularity of zebrafish is driven by recent advancements in brain imaging, molecular genetic manipulation, and behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Parichy, 2015).

claim: The increased popularity of zebrafish is driven by recent advancements in brain imaging, molecular genetic manipulation, and behavior.
source: Originally established as a model organism for developmental biology due to ease of domestication, high fecundity, and early life transparency (Parichy, 2015), the increased popularity of zebrafish is driven by recent advancements in brain imaging, molecular genetic manipulation, and behavior.
evidence: This reflects knowledge about recent trends in zebrafish research.

claim: Several digital atlases exist for larval zebrafish.
source: Although several digital atlases exist for larval zebrafish (Kunst et al., 2019; Randlett et al., 2015; Ronneberger et al., 2012; Tabor et al., 2019), no atlas of equivalent detail has been created for adult zebrafish.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on larval zebrafish atlases.

claim: No atlas of equivalent detail has been created for adult zebrafish prior to AZBA.
source: Although several digital atlases exist for larval zebrafish (Kunst et al., 2019; Randlett et al., 2015; Ronneberger et al., 2012; Tabor et al., 2019), no atlas of equivalent detail has been created for adult zebrafish.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work, inferred from the absence of prior comparable resources.

claim: Adult zebrafish provide several important advantages over larval zebrafish such as a mature and histologically differentiated neuroanatomy and a rich behavioral repertoire.
source: Adult zebrafish provide several important advantages over larval zebrafish such as a mature and histologically differentiated neuroanatomy and a rich behavioral repertoire that includes long-term associative memory, complex social interactions, and goal-driven behaviors (Gerlai, 2016; Kalueff et al., 2013; Kenney et al., 2017; Nakajo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Adult zebrafish exhibit long-term associative memory, complex social interactions, and goal-driven behaviors.
source: Adult zebrafish provide several important advantages over larval zebrafish such as a mature and histologically differentiated neuroanatomy and a rich behavioral repertoire that includes long-term associative memory, complex social interactions, and goal-driven behaviors (Gerlai, 2016; Kalueff et al., 2013; Kenney et al., 2017; Nakajo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: 3D digital brain atlases are essential tools for modern neuroscience.
source: 3D digital brain atlases are essential tools for modern neuroscience because they facilitate lines of inquiry that are not possible with two-dimensional book-based atlases.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the utility of digital atlases in neuroscience.

claim: Visualization of the 3D structure of the brain and incorporation of new data or discoveries are difficult, if not impossible, with a print atlas.
source: For example, visualization of the 3D structure of the brain and incorporation of new data or discoveries are difficult, if not impossible, with a print atlas.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of print media compared to digital formats.

claim: Digital atlases enable exploration of brain structures in any arbitrary 3D perspective.
source: In contrast, digital atlases enable exploration of brain structures in any arbitrary 3D perspective and can be readily updated to incorporate new information such as patterns of gene expression and anatomical connectivity, as has been done for the mouse (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of digital atlas capabilities and supported by a citation to mouse atlas work.

claim: Digital atlases can be readily updated to incorporate new information such as patterns of gene expression and anatomical connectivity.
source: In contrast, digital atlases enable exploration of brain structures in any arbitrary 3D perspective and can be readily updated to incorporate new information such as patterns of gene expression and anatomical connectivity, as has been done for the mouse (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on mouse atlases.

claim: A digital atlas would enhance the use of adult zebrafish in disease modeling by enabling a more comprehensive understanding of how the brain changes in response to insults.
source: A digital atlas would also enhance the use of adult zebrafish in disease modeling by enabling a more comprehensive understanding of how the brain changes in response to insults that occur in neurodevelopmental disorders (Sakai et al., 2018), traumatic brain injury (McCutcheon et al., 2017), neurodegeneration (Xi et al., 2011), and the formation and spreading of gliomas (Idilli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications, supported by citations to disease modeling studies.

claim: Digital atlases enable automated segmentation of new images.
source: Finally, digital atlases enable automated segmentation of new images, which is essential for whole brain mapping approaches that can lead to unexpected discoveries of regional function (Bahl and Engert, 2020; Kim et al., 2015; Pantoja et al., 2020; Randlett et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on whole brain mapping.

claim: Automated segmentation is essential for whole brain mapping approaches that can lead to unexpected discoveries of regional function.
source: Finally, digital atlases enable automated segmentation of new images, which is essential for whole brain mapping approaches that can lead to unexpected discoveries of regional function (Bahl and Engert, 2020; Kim et al., 2015; Pantoja et al., 2020; Randlett et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating this capability.

claim: Whole brain activity mapping facilitates powerful network approaches to understanding brain function.
source: Whole brain activity mapping also facilitates powerful network approaches to understanding brain (Bassett and Sporns, 2017; Coelho et al., 2018; Vetere et al., 2017; Wheeler et al., 2013), yielding insight into how coordinated brain-wide activity gives rise to behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on brain network analysis.

claim: The mature adult zebrafish brain is opaque and an order of magnitude larger than the larval brain.
source: The generation of a brain atlas for adult zebrafish presents several challenges in comparison to the larval brain because the mature brain is opaque and an order of magnitude larger; this makes traditional whole-mount approaches impossible and confocal or wide-field microscopy infeasible.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of zebrafish developmental biology and physical properties.

claim: The opacity and size of the adult zebrafish brain makes traditional whole-mount approaches impossible and confocal or wide-field microscopy infeasible.
source: The generation of a brain atlas for adult zebrafish presents several challenges in comparison to the larval brain because the mature brain is opaque and an order of magnitude larger; this makes traditional whole-mount approaches impossible and confocal or wide-field microscopy infeasible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical limitations of these techniques given the properties of adult zebrafish brains.

claim: Adult brains were rendered transparent using a tissue clearing approach (iDISCO+).
source: To enable whole-mount imaging, we rendered adult brains transparent using a tissue clearing approach (iDISCO+) that is compatible with different stains such as small molecules, antibodies, and in situ probes (Kramer et al., 2018; Renier et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, supported by citations to the iDISCO+ technique.

claim: iDISCO+ is compatible with different stains such as small molecules, antibodies, and in situ probes.
source: To enable whole-mount imaging, we rendered adult brains transparent using a tissue clearing approach (iDISCO+) that is compatible with different stains such as small molecules, antibodies, and in situ probes (Kramer et al., 2018; Renier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on iDISCO+.

claim: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy was used for rapid large volume imaging with minimal photobleaching.
source: High-resolution imaging of samples as large as intact adult brains is not amenable to conventional microscopic techniques, so we turned to light-sheet fluorescence microscopy for rapid large volume imaging with minimal photobleaching (Pitrone et al., 2013; Reynaud et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by citations to prior work on light-sheet microscopy.

claim: 3D volumes from multiple animals were registered into the same anatomical space prior to averaging to generate an atlas that minimizes individual variations in neuroanatomy.
source: To generate an atlas that minimizes individual variations in neuroanatomy, we registered 3D volumes from multiple animals into the same anatomical space prior to averaging (Lerch et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by a citation to prior work on image registration.

claim: Images from 10 different antibody stains were registered into the same anatomical space to help guide segmentation and generate insight into the neurochemical organization of the brain.
source: To help guide segmentation and generate insight into the neurochemical organization of the brain, images from 10 different antibody stains were also registered into the same anatomical space.
evidence: This describes the methodology and data collected in the study.

claim: Manual segmentation was performed, delineating the atlas into over 200 neuroanatomical regions, including nuclei and white matter tracts.
source: Finally, we performed manual segmentation, delineating the atlas into over 200 neuroanatomical regions, including nuclei and white matter tracts.
evidence: This describes the methodology and results of the segmentation process.

claim: AZBA is the most comprehensive, detailed, and up-to-date atlas of the adult zebrafish brain.
source: Taken together, AZBA is the most comprehensive, detailed, and up-to-date atlas of the adult zebrafish brain.
evidence: This is a claim about the quality and novelty of the work, inferred from the comprehensive methodology and results presented.

claim: All averaged images are freely available at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.dfn2z351g and azba.wayne.edu.
source: We have made all averaged images freely available (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.dfn2z351g; azba.wayne.edu) to enable their use in exploring the organization of the zebrafish brain and automated segmentation for activity mapping.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: AZBA can be continuously updated to reflect the latest findings in zebrafish neuroanatomy because it was generated using readily available techniques.
source: By generating this resource using readily available techniques, AZBA can be continuously updated to reflect the latest findings in zebrafish neuroanatomy.
evidence: This is an inference about the updatability of the resource based on the methodology used.

claim: AZBA will become an indispensable resource as adult zebrafish continue to gain traction as a model organism in understanding the intricacies of the vertebrate brain.
source: We anticipate this becoming an indispensable resource as adult zebrafish continue to gain traction as a model organism in understanding the intricacies of the vertebrate brain.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the future impact of the resource.

claim: A whole-mount preparation was used to avoid issues with slice-based techniques such as tissue loss, tearing, and distortion.
source: We used a whole-mount preparation to avoid issues with slice-based techniques such as tissue loss, tearing, and distortion.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the methodology used.

claim: iDISCO+ is a rapid organic solvent-based tissue clearing technique that renders brains optically transparent.
source: To circumvent the challenge of tissue opacity, we used a rapid organic solvent-based tissue clearing technique, iDISCO+ (Renier et al., 2016), that renders brains optically transparent.
evidence: This describes the technique used, supported by a citation.

claim: Tissue clearing using iDISCO+ resulted in transparent brains.
source: Tissue clearing using iDISCO+ resulted in transparent brains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cleared and stained brains were imaged in the horizontal plane with an in-plane resolution of 3.25 μm and an axial step size of 4 μm.
source: Cleared and stained brains were imaged in the horizontal plane with an in-plane resolution of 3.25 μm and an axial step size of 4 μm (Figure 2B) yielding near-isotropic signals at sufficient resolution to clearly distinguish regional boundaries.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters used in the study.

claim: The imaging yielded near-isotropic signals at sufficient resolution to clearly distinguish regional boundaries.
source: Cleared and stained brains were imaged in the horizontal plane with an in-plane resolution of 3.25 μm and an axial step size of 4 μm (Figure 2B) yielding near-isotropic signals at sufficient resolution to clearly distinguish regional boundaries.
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging parameters and quality of the resulting images.

claim: 17 sets of nuclear-stained and associated autofluorescence images from both male and female fish (eight females) were retained for registration.
source: We retained 17 sets of nuclear-stained and associated autofluorescence images from both male and female fish (eight females), each of which were transformed into 3D volumes for registration.
evidence: This describes the sample size and composition used in the study.

claim: The atlas was generated by registering images from individual animals into the same space, thereby creating an anatomical average.
source: The atlas was generated by registering images from individual animals into the same space, thereby creating an anatomical average.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to create the atlas.

claim: The image registration approach has been previously used in humans, mice, macaques, and zebrafish larvae.
source: This approach has been previously used in humans (Klein et al., 2009), mice (Dorr et al., 2008; Steadman et al., 2014), macaques (McLaren et al., 2009), and zebrafish larvae (Kunst et al., 2019; Randlett et al., 2015; Ronneberger et al., 2012; Tabor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work using similar registration approaches.

claim: The registration method begins with a 6-parameter linear registration to rotate and translate the initial image dataset.
source: This method begins with a 6-parameter linear registration to rotate and translate the initial image dataset followed by a 12-parameter affine registration to scale, translate, rotate, and shear the dataset with a pairwise approach to avoid bias by outlier images (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: A 12-parameter affine registration was performed to scale, translate, rotate, and shear the dataset with a pairwise approach to avoid bias by outlier images.
source: This method begins with a 6-parameter linear registration to rotate and translate the initial image dataset followed by a 12-parameter affine registration to scale, translate, rotate, and shear the dataset with a pairwise approach to avoid bias by outlier images (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: An iterative nonlinear registration with six iterations at subsequently higher resolutions was performed using minctracc.
source: Lastly, an iterative nonlinear registration with six iterations at subsequently higher resolutions was performed using minctracc (Collins and Evans, 2011).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by a citation to the minctracc tool.

claim: The registration resulted in a set of linear and nonlinear transformations for each TO-PRO image from native space to a consensus space and orientation.
source: This resulted in a set of linear and nonlinear transformations for each TO-PRO image in our dataset from native space to a consensus space and orientation.
evidence: This describes the output of the registration process.

claim: The transformations were applied to corresponding autofluorescence images, creating an atlas with averaged images containing TO-PRO and autofluorescence signals.
source: These transformations were then applied to corresponding autofluorescence images, thereby creating an atlas with averaged images containing TO-PRO and autofluorescence signals (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the methodology and results, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Images were acquired using 10 different antibody stains to provide additional guidance for segmentation and generate insight into the neurochemical organization of the adult zebrafish brain.
source: To provide additional guidance for segmentation and generate insight into the neurochemical organization of the adult zebrafish brain, we also acquired images using 10 different antibody stains (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the methodology and rationale for using antibody stains.

claim: The antibody stains used identify different cell types in the brain, such as neurons (HuC/D), radial glial cells (GFAP), and proliferating cells (PCNA).
source: We sought stains that would identify different cell types in the brain, such as neurons (HuC/D), radial glial cells (glial fibrillary associated protein [GFAP]), and proliferating cells (proliferating cell nuclear antigen [PCNA]), markers for different neurotransmitters (tyrosine hydroxylase [TH], 5-hydroxytryptamine [5-HT], and choline acetyltransferase [ChAT]), and calcium binding proteins (parvalbumin [PV], calbindin, and calretinin).
evidence: This describes the types of antibody stains used and their targets.

claim: Some antibody stains, such as TH, 5-HT, ChAT, and calretinin, have already been subject to brain-wide analysis, making them useful for guiding segmentation.
source: Some of these stains, such as TH, 5-HT, ChAT, and calretinin, have already been subject to brain-wide analysis, making them useful for guiding segmentation.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from prior literature on these stains.

claim: Autofluorescence images from antibody stains were registered with the autofluorescence channel of the TO-PRO images to bring antibody stains into the same anatomical space as the TO-PRO stain.
source: Autofluorescence images from antibody stains were registered with the autofluorescence channel of the TO-PRO images, yielding a set of transformations that were used to bring antibody stains into the same anatomical space as the TO-PRO stain (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: At least five independent brains were averaged together to generate a representative image for each antibody.
source: To generate a representative image for each antibody, we averaged together at least five independent brains.
evidence: This describes the sample size used for each antibody stain.

claim: The approach resulted in strong correspondence between antibody images and the TO-PRO stain.
source: Our approach resulted in strong correspondence between antibody images and the TO-PRO stain (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a qualitative assessment of the registration quality, illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: Using a mixed-model ANOVA, a main effect of signal was found (F(1,13) = 1084, p=6.6 × 10–14) with the TO-PRO signal having greater mean precision (15 ± 10 µm vs. 99 ± 53 µm).
source: Using a mixed-model ANOVA (2 × 15; signal [between subject] × landmark [within subject]), we found a main effect of signal (F(1,13) = 1084, p=6.6 × 10–14) with the TO-PRO signal having greater mean precision (15 ± 10 µm vs. 99 ± 53 µm; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of registration precision data.

claim: There was a significant effect of landmark (F(5,65) = 98, p<2 × 10–16) and an interaction between signal and landmark (F(5, 65) = 120, p<2 × 10–16) in registration precision.
source: However, there was also a significant effect of landmark (F(5,65) = 98, p<2 × 10–16), and an interaction between signal and landmark (F(5, 65) = 120, p<2 × 10–16).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of registration precision data.

claim: In the autofluorescence images, the average precision of each landmark covers a much wider range (17–180 µm) than TO-PRO (9–23 µm).
source: A closer examination of the data revealed that in the autofluorescence images the average precision of each landmark covers a much wider range (17–180 µm) than TO-PRO (9–23 µm).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the registration precision data.

claim: The larger error measured using autofluorescence images is likely due to experimenter error in selecting points, reflecting the paucity of well-defined landmarks in this signal compared to the richer, high-contrast TO-PRO images.
source: This suggests that the larger error measured using autofluorescence images is likely due to experimenter error in selecting points, reflecting the paucity of well-defined landmarks in this signal compared to the richer, high-contrast TO-PRO images.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of the precision data.

claim: Segmentation was primarily guided by the seminal atlas of Wullimann et al., 1996.
source: Segmentation was primarily guided by the seminal atlas of Wullimann et al., 1996.
evidence: This describes the primary reference used for segmentation.

claim: Regional boundaries and terminology were updated for parts of the brain that have been subject to more recent analysis such as the telencephalon, hypothalamic regions, and motor nuclei.
source: Regional boundaries and terminology were updated for parts of the brain that have been subject to more recent analysis such as the telencephalon, hypothalamic regions, and motor nuclei (Mueller et al., 2004; Porter and Mueller, 2020; Rink and Wullimann, 2001).
evidence: This describes updates to the segmentation based on more recent literature, supported by citations.

claim: Segmenting large, clearly delineated regions, such as the optic tectum and the cerebellum, was straightforward.
source: Segmenting large, clearly delineated regions, such as the optic tectum and the cerebellum, was straightforward (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a qualitative assessment of the segmentation process.

claim: Small nuclei that only appear in one or two slices in the atlas or in images from only one axis proved more challenging to segment.
source: Small nuclei that only appear in one or two slices in the atlas or in images from only one axis proved more challenging.
evidence: This is a qualitative assessment of the challenges in the segmentation process.

claim: The coronal axis was primarily used for segmenting small nuclei due to it being the most extensively represented in both the atlas and the literature.
source: For such regions, we primarily made use of the coronal axis due to it being the most extensively represented in both the atlas and the literature (Figure 5A, bottom).
evidence: This describes the rationale for using the coronal axis in segmentation.

claim: A neuronal marker (HuC/D) was used in conjunction with the nuclear stain to safely identify many boundaries.
source: To ensure we captured as many neuronal structures as possible, we also made extensive use of a neuronal marker (HuC/D) in conjunction with the nuclear stain, which allowed us to safely identify many boundaries (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology used for segmentation.

claim: The original brain atlas contains a significant amount of unsegmented space.
source: Other challenges included the fact that the original brain atlas contains a significant amount of unsegmented space.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of the prior atlas.

claim: Unsegmented regions were labeled as 'unknown' and according to their lowest anatomical level.
source: We labeled these regions as 'unknown' and according to their lowest anatomical level (e.g., unknown ventral telencephalon [UnkVT], unknown diencephalon [UnkD], etc.).
evidence: This describes the labeling convention used for unsegmented regions.

claim: Identification of tracts was largely based on a combination of autofluorescence and lack of nuclear and neuronal staining since a white matter stain compatible with iDISCO+ was not found.
source: Identification of tracts was largely based on a combination of autofluorescence and lack of nuclear and neuronal staining since we were unsuccessful in finding a white matter stain compatible with iDISCO+ (e.g., the MLF: Figure 4D, pink arrowheads).
evidence: This describes the methodology and challenges in identifying white matter tracts.

claim: All immunostainings showed high overlap with prior work, establishing the validity of these antibodies.
source: All of our immunostainings showed high overlap with prior work, establishing the validity of these antibodies (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a qualitative assessment of the antibody staining results compared to prior literature.

claim: Extensive TH expression was found in the olfactory bulb and as a continuous band ventral to the Dc region in the telencephalon.
source: For example, in the telencephalon we found extensive TH expression in the olfactory bulb (Figure 5Ba), and as a continuous band ventral to the Dc region (Figure 5Bb).
evidence: This describes the observed TH expression pattern, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TH staining was elevated in the optic tectum, thalamic, and hypothalamic regions, the LC, and in the XLo of the hindbrain.
source: As previously reported, TH staining was also elevated in the optic tectum, thalamic, and hypothalamic regions (Figure 5Bc,d), the LC (Figure 5Be), and in the XLo of the hindbrain (Figure 5Bf).
evidence: This describes the observed TH expression pattern, consistent with prior reports.

claim: 5-HT staining was more diffuse in regions like the optic tectum and the dorsal part of the telencephalon, with pockets of high expression restricted to regions like the PVO, PTN, posterior portion of the Hc, and the SR.
source: We found 5-HT staining to be more diffuse in regions like the optic tectum and the dorsal part of the telencephalon (Figure 5Ca,b), with pockets of high expression restricted to regions like the PVO (Figure 5Cc), PTN (Figure 5Cd), posterior portion of the Hc (Figure 5Ce), and the SR (Figure 5Cf).
evidence: This describes the observed 5-HT expression pattern, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ChAT staining was clearly discerned in places such as the RT, near the TTB, and in the SRN and NLV.
source: Using ChAT, we could clearly discern staining in places such as the RT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Ba), near the TTB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Bb), and in the SRN and NLV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Bc).
evidence: This describes the observed ChAT expression pattern, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ChAT staining was apparent in several motor nuclei such as the OENr and VIIm, OENc, and IXm.
source: ChAT staining was also apparent in several motor nuclei such as the OENr and VIIm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Bd), OENc (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Be), and IXm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Be).
evidence: This describes the observed ChAT expression pattern in motor nuclei, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: High levels of calretinin staining were seen in the olfactory bulb, the Dm, the PSP and optic tract, optic tectum, the TLa, SG, TGN, and anterior portion of the DIL, with particularly strong staining in the SGN and DON.
source: Finally, examples of high levels of calretinin staining can be seen in the olfactory bulb (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Ca), the Dm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cb), the PSP and optic tract (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cc), optic tectum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cc–e), the TLa, SG, TGN, and anterior portion of the DIL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cd) with particularly strong staining in the SGN (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Ce) and DON (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cf).
evidence: This describes the observed calretinin expression pattern, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The segmentation resulted in a 3D model of the zebrafish brain that can be viewed from any arbitrary angle.
source: Our segmentation resulted in a 3D model of the zebrafish brain that can be viewed from any arbitrary angle (Figure 5D).
evidence: This describes the output of the segmentation process, illustrated in Figure 5D.

claim: Each nucleus, white matter tract, ventricle, and anatomical space was given a unique abbreviation and color, totaling 203 regions.
source: Each nucleus, white matter tract, ventricle, and anatomical space was given a unique abbreviation and color, totaling 203 regions (Supplementary file 1) and associated with an anatomical hierarchy (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This describes the organization and labeling of the segmented regions.

claim: The full extent of the atlas can be appreciated using the website (azba.wayne.edu) or ITK-SNAP.
source: The full extent of the atlas can be appreciated using the website (azba.wayne.edu) or ITK-SNAP (Yushkevich et al., 2019), a freely available software package designed for viewing 3D medical images that allows for the simultaneous viewing of the stains and segmentation in the coronal, sagittal, and horizontal planes (Figure 6).

claim: All files for exploring AZBA are freely available for use in ITK-SNAP or other programs at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.dfn2z351g.
source: All files for exploring AZBA are freely available for use in ITK-SNAP or other programs (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.dfn2z351g).
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: Images from both male and female fish were combined to generate a representative brain.
source: Because the goal of the atlas was to generate a representative brain, we combined images from both male and female fish.

claim: Using a mixed-model ANOVA, neither an effect of sex (F(1,15) = 0.11, p=0.75) nor an interaction between sex and brain region (F(202, 3030) = 0.14, p=1) was found.
source: To determine if there was an effect of sex on brain volumes in our TO-PRO image set, we used a mixed-model ANOVA (2 × 203; sex [between subjects] × brain region [within subjects]). We found neither an effect of sex (F(1,15) = 0.11, p=0.75; Figure 5—figure supplement 2) nor an interaction between sex and brain region (F(202, 3030) = 0.14, p=1; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that sex did not affect the overall size of the brain or individual regions.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of sex differences in brain volumes.

claim: Sex did not affect the overall size of the brain or individual regions.
source: We found neither an effect of sex (F(1,15) = 0.11, p=0.75; Figure 5—figure supplement 2) nor an interaction between sex and brain region (F(202, 3030) = 0.14, p=1; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that sex did not affect the overall size of the brain or individual regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of brain volumes.

claim: A main effect of region was found (F(202, 3030) = 495, p<2 × 10–16), consistent with the wide range of region sizes observed across the brain (0.000026–0.53 mm3).
source: We did find a main effect of region (F(202, 3030) = 495, p<2 × 10–16), consistent with the wide range of region sizes observed across the brain (0.000026–0.53 mm3; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of regional brain volumes.

claim: Parvalbumin (PV) is a calcium binding protein that labels a class of inhibitory interneurons.
source: Parvalbumin (PV) is a calcium binding protein that labels a class of inhibitory interneurons (Celio, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on parvalbumin.
